title: Ya-Sin, heart of the book
hook: often recited for the dying and on Thursday nights in many communities
tomorrow: The man from the city's edge

segments.voice: Yesterday: white, red and black mountains, and those who know standing in awe. Your line was knowledge brings awe.

A hospital room, late. A grandmother is very ill, and the family has gathered. Someone opens a small, worn booklet, or a phone, and begins to recite in Arabic, softly, steadily. In a mosque across town, it's Thursday evening, and a circle of people is reciting the same words. In a cemetery, someone stands by a grave and reads it again. In many Muslim communities, this is the surah people reach for at the edges of life. It begins with two letters: Ya. Sin.

Surah thirty-six, eighty-three verses. Its name is its first verse: two Arabic letters, ya and sin, said by themselves, like the disconnected letters that open a number of surahs. What they mean, many scholars say, Allah knows best. Some say Ya-Sin is a name for the Prophet ﷺ, and it's also a boy's name. The text doesn't say. Then, Pickthall: "By the wise Qur'an, Lo! thou art of those sent". An oath on the book itself, and a reassurance to the Prophet that he's a real messenger. Why is it called the heart of the Qur'an? A hadith in the collection of al-Tirmidhi says everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Another, in Abu Dawud, says recite Ya-Sin over your dying. The honest part: many hadith scholars grade both reports as weak in their chains. Others accept them, or point to the surah's content. And the content speaks to what a family at a bedside may want to hear: it says the messengers were true, that the dead will be raised, that the One who made a person the first time can make them again. Its closing verses ask, can't He who created the heavens and the earth create their like? At a bedside, that's not abstract theology. It's a promise said aloud in a hard room. So Ya-Sin earned its place in many communities on two grounds: reports some accept and some question, and a message everyone can hear. Over the next three days, this path opens it.

segments.voice: If you can, play the opening of a recitation of Ya-Sin in Arabic and simply listen, whether or not you follow the words, noticing how many verses end on the same sound. If you can't play it now, sit and remember someone you've lost, or someone who's ill, and hold them quietly in mind.
Ya-Sin. Surah thirty-six, named for its two opening letters, recited for the dying and on Thursday nights in many communities. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of the book. Its first words are just two letters. Until tomorrow.

fork.reveal: Ya-Sin, following a hadith in Abu Dawud that some scholars accept and others grade weak, and a message about rising again.

what a scholar hears: 'the heart of the Qur'an' is Tirmidhi 2887 and 'recite it over your dying' is Abu Dawud 3121; both chains are debated, while the surah's themes of messengers and resurrection fit the custom.

chat.says: Why do Muslim families sometimes recite Ya-Sin beside someone who is dying?
options: Reports call it the heart of the Qur'an, and it says the dead will be raised.
Because reciting it is believed to delay death by a few more days.
Because it's one of the shortest surahs, so it's easy to finish in time.
chat.meaning: Hadith reports, graded differently by scholars, call Ya-Sin the heart of the Qur'an, and its message speaks to a bedside: the dead will be raised.
